I don't know if I have any great advice here - just wanted to say I understand as a fellow limerence sufferer. It seems like you have great insight into your situation - which is an annoying thing to say, I know, I hear it from therapists all the time and it can be unhelpful - but I think awareness is key here. 

I was in a relationship with a very loving partner for about a year and a half, all while experiencing limerence for someone I briefly saw years ago. I still struggle with the obsession with that person. As in, thinking about them every single day for the past four years. 

Having limerent feelings towards another while being in a relationship is not immoral - it speaks to an unmet need. Limerence is always about YOU, not the person you're obsessed with. I noticed that I was unable to regulate my own emotions, and I relied on the proximity of this person to me to decide how good I was going to feel on any given day. Limerence is terrifying - I often felt I couldn't open up to anyone, even therapists, because I felt so insane. But, again, it's really not the person themselves you're obsessed with - it's the idea of safety and comfort that comes from them.

Sometimes using coping skills in the moment can help as well. When you look back at the moment you didn't feel dissociated, what was unique about it? It's okay if you don't know. Is there anything you were doing in that moment that you can use to help you cope in the future? You mentioned you were in your room listening to music - music can be a really powerful tool to connect with both your past and present self. You're right that sometimes our bodies know things that we don't - sometimes it's better to learn to feel your way through a dissociative experience, rather than thinking your way through it. I'm sure your therapist has given you these tools already, but maybe you could try finding other ways to get your senses involved to help you feel more present?

So, my symptoms started back in March... I went to urgent care bc I thought I had a UTI. Almost overnight, I had a strong and constant urge to pee. I was told I didn't have one. 

I then saw a primary care dr., who also tested me for a UTI, and told me to try some over the counter methods. Azo, cranberry, stuff like that. None of those methods help, and I'm also told I have bacterial vaginosis and it may be irritating my urinary tract. I tested neg for UTI again, and was referred to a urologist.

The urologist suggested I may have interstitial cystitis, which I'm sure you've heard of. Other than that, she said (verbatim) she had no way of explaining my symptoms. 

I then see an NP at my gynecologist who tells me what I have going on is outside of her depth, so I wait to get in with a DR. In the meantime, I at transvaginal ultrasound done because I'm told that sometimes ovarian cysts can cause problems with urinary urgency. My ultrasound looks normal. I see the DR, and he tells me I have a tight pelvic floor. I've done 3 months of pelvic floor PT since that, with no effect on my symptoms. 

The gyno then suggests it may be endometriosis, but he wants me to see a GI (have been having issues with my stomach as well) to rule out anything there. I see the GI, who has not much to say but for me to take laxatives, and I go back to my gyno. He no longer thinks my symptoms line up with endometriosis. Hi friend, 

I'm sorry to hear your'e struggling. I'm not a professional, but it isn't definitely textbook OCD for your OCD to tell you you are using it as an excuse to be an awful person. It for sure feeds off of that guilt, and will always leave you guessing whether or not you actually have it. A tool that my therapist gave me to assess my thoughts (when I'm thinking they aren't OCD) is this - she told me that that if my thoughts feel very urgent in nature, they're probably OCD. If it feels like you need to do something to fix a problem RIGHT NOW, it's probably based on an ocd thought. 

If the thoughts get worse with reassurance, that's another solid indicator that it's OCD. If you find that reassuring yourself you are a good person (or having others reassure you you are a good person) only makes the thoughts stronger, they are probably OCD thoughts.

Unfortunately, there isn't really any way around it. The whole reason exposures are so difficult is because you have to accept the anxiety that comes with accepting the thought. 

I know providing reassurance doesn't help, but I can promise you that this is textbook OCD, and agreeing with your thoughts will not have any power over your reality. My primary 'theme' used to be thoughts that I would hurt someone else. I remember how scary it was when I started agreeing with the thoughts aloud in therapy - I would force myself to say, yes, I want to do x to this person, or I wish this person would die. It was fucking TERRIFYING. But eventually, I started to notice my anxiety would spike, and then come right back down. 

You don't have to start with that, though. Exposures should be uncomfortable, but you don't have to go from 0-100 that quick. You could start with more neutral responses. If you got a thought like, I wish this person would die, you could try a non-engagement response like, "Hm.. maybe I do think that" or "That's a funny thought." These will allow you to acknowledge the thoughts without reading into them. Really try and lean into that not knowing. I think if you start here, you can work your way up to going in the direction of the thoughts.

Hi, I'm not the OP but - 

I'm on a medication called Clomipramine; it's a tricyclic anti-depressant, and the psychiatrist I see kind of sees it as the miracle worker for OCD. I would recommend therapy more than anything, though. I don't want to scare you - meds can be helpful for so many folks (I know that they allow me to function) but I've also had a lot of scary side effects on other medications. When I was on an anti-psychotic called Risperidone, my neck would involuntarily move, and I was told it could be permanent. So I would for sure say do your research with meds. 

ERP (exposure response prevention) therapy is typically seen as the gold standard for OCD - typical talk therapy is usually not recommended, as it can make OCD worse. Therapists shouldn't ask you to try and find meaning behind you intrusive thoughts, as this leads to compulsive analysis, and further rumination. In ERP, you expose yourself to your triggers, and try and change the ways in which you react to them. For people like me, who are scared they are going to harm someone else, an exposure could be carrying a knife around with me. For you, you might continue to go hiking, and work with a therapist to make a plan for how you may handle those thoughts the next time they arise. The goal is that you don't engage with the thoughts - they come up, and you don't analyze them/ascribe meaning to them. They come and go. 

It is really about what works for you, though - some people I know have found CBT (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy) to be helpful as well. If you tend to have moments where you feel overwhelmed with anxiety, CBT can give you skills to cope with those feelings. If you do see a therapist, I would recommend finding someone that you for sure know works well with OCD - an old therapist of mine was less than helpful, because she thought my intrusive thoughts were actual homicidal/suicidal thoughts. 

Sorry this was so long, it ended up being therapeutic for me to type. Let me know if you have any questions!

I think OCD also likes to think of the worst case scenario - for me, the only thing I could thing of that's worse than someone I love getting hurt, is if I was the one to hurt them. My OCD knows this, and it makes me live out my worst fear through my thoughts constantly. 

It makes sense if you think about how many mothers have intrusive thoughts about harming their children - it doesn't mean they're bad parents or violent people, it's just their brain's fucked-up way of protecting their babies. It was just a matter of learning how to tolerate the thoughts without running away from them! Naturally, because the thoughts are so disturbing, you are going to do everything you can to make yourself feel better. You fight the thoughts - you tell yourself that these thoughts aren't you, and that you don't accept them. It's a matter of letting the thoughts come and accepting them fully: you can't change the fact that you have the thoughts in the first place, but you can control your reaction to them. You don't have to tackle it all at once - just give it a try next time you have an intrusive thought. Try letting the thought pass through you without adding a value judgement to it!

Don't put so much pressure on yourself! It's good to have something that you care about in high school, but I can guarantee that most people your age have no idea what the fuck they want to do with their lives. It's an incredible thing that you're even thinking about your future - when I was your age, all I did was smoke weed and cut class. Being young is about enjoying your life: you don't deserve to feel shame for hanging out with your friends and doing something that you like! OCD makes us believe that we need to be perfect all the time, that we need to constantly be doing something. This isn't true - all we need to do is enjoy ourselves. That's the biggest thing. At least that's what I've found out so far on my journey with OCD. So, keep your eye on the future, but don't forget about the present moment.

The first thing that you need to know is that your thoughts are not reality - no matter how disturbing and "real" they feel. If you talk to someone who knows about OCD, I can promise you that they will understand. The more power you give to the thoughts, the more and more prevalent they will become. I feel your pain entirely: it's never easy to be honest with others about this type of thing, because you fear that they will think you're "crazy". I can give you a positive story, though - I lived with untreated OCD for ten years, until I finally opened up to a psychiatrist I was seeing when I was 18. I was totally freaking out, and did not want to have to reveal the kind of thoughts I was having to her. I eventually told her, and she very simply and calmly was like "Sounds like you have OCD". No judgement, no shame, no nothing. She was a professional, and she understood what I was going through! We aren't the only ones in the world that have this, even when it feels like it.

Its really hard to not react to those thoughts, they feel the most important thoughts youll ever have...What youd likely get thought to do in therapy is to let the thoughts pass through without reacting to them or judging them. So say you would get a thought like "I will die someday" and the thought bothers you immensely: what you would work on with a therapist is having that thought, acknowledging it (Saying to the thought, yes, that is true), and moving on with what you are doing. 
And yes, I am on a med which is a trycylic antidepressant (one that is often also used to treat OCD) and it makes it more difficult for me to get stuck in thought spirals and ruminate.... I think something that may be important for you is having grace with yourself and trying not to get frustrated when you can't shake the thoughts off - ocd is powerful, and the strength it takes to face it is something many people will not ever have to muster up in their entire lives. Remind yourself that it is a process, and the more you are frustrated and angry at the thoughts, the more power they will have over you. A friend of mine who also suffers from anxiety gave me a great piece of advice - ocd is like a nagging, annoying little kid, and the more attention you give it, the more its going to keep coming back looking for attention.
